stages.name: Emerging and developing economies: primary industry, Fairtrade and trade liberalisation
stages.title: Emerging and developing economies
stages.sub: After this, the student can explain why relying on primary industries is risky, how Fairtrade tries to fix that, its own limits, and why opening up trade can make dependency worse.

steps.q: A country earns almost all its export income from selling raw coffee beans. A frost destroys half the world's coffee crop and the price triples overnight. Does this country's export income stay steady?
steps.right: No, it swings wildly with the price
steps.wrong: Yes, it stays roughly the same
steps.hint: Think about what already happens to commodity prices, and what that does to a country that relies on just one export.

steps.q: Farmers in a poor country sell coffee beans to a buyer who promises to pay at least a fixed minimum, however low the world price falls, plus an extra sum for the farmers to invest in their community. What does this arrangement protect the farmers from?
steps.right: A collapse in the world price
steps.wrong: A rise in the world price
steps.hint: The buyer is guaranteeing a floor price and an extra premium, not simply letting the free market set the price.

steps.q: The world coffee price crashes, but these farmers still receive the guaranteed minimum plus the premium for a new well. What has this protected them from?
steps.right: The income losses caused by volatile prices
steps.wrong: The need to grow any coffee at all
steps.hint: Look back at what a guaranteed minimum price actually shields the farmer against when the market price falls.

steps.q: Only a small fraction of the extra price paid by shoppers for Fairtrade coffee actually reaches the farmers, and only certain certified producers can join the scheme at all. Does everyone who grows coffee benefit equally?
steps.right: No, many farmers gain little or are excluded
steps.hint: Think about certification costs and who gets to join, versus who is left out.

steps.q: A developing country removes its tariffs and fully opens up to trade. Cheap manufactured imports now flood in and out-compete its small factories, so the country ends up exporting even more raw cotton than before, and importing manufactured cloth. Has its reliance on one raw export gone down or up?
steps.hint: If local manufacturing cannot survive the competition, what is left for the country to sell abroad?
